abstract: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) is a post-transcriptional surveillance pathway that degrades aberrant transcripts harboring premature termination codons. Thereby, NMD also limits the abundance of transcripts encoding potentially immunogenic peptides. Here, we investigated whether pharmacological inhibition of the NMD kinase SMG1 remodels the human leukocyte antigen class I (HLA-I) immunopeptidome and enhances immune recognition of H838 non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cells. Treatment with a SMG1 inhibitor (SMG1i) effectively perturbed NMD, as reflected by increased abundance of NMD-sensitive transcripts. To identify NMD inhibition-associated HLA-I peptides beyond the canonical proteome, long-read RNA sequencing and ribosome profiling were integrated to generate a cell-specific sequence database for immunopeptidomic analysis. Identified peptides were further evaluated using an extended metascore incorporating predicted HLA binding and proteasomal processing to define a high-confidence HLA-I peptide repertoire. Of the 2,728 peptides passing the 1% false discovery rate threshold, 48 were detected exclusively in SMG1i-treated samples. Of these, 32 fulfilled additional criteria for recurrence, peptide length, and predicted binding to the genotyped H838 HLA-I alleles. The observed changes in HLA-I-bound immunopeptides were not accompanied by an increase in global surface HLA-I abundance, suggesting remodeling of peptide composition rather than increased HLA-I presentation capacity. Exploratory allogeneic co-culture experiments showed SMG1i-induced IFN-{gamma} response in partially HLA-matched CD8 T-cells compared with an unmatched donor and increased expression of effector-associated genes. Together, these findings establish a cell-specific, proteogenomic, and HLA-informed framework for identifying SMG1i-associated HLA-I peptides in an NSCLC model and prioritizing candidates for peptide-specific functional validation.
